plan: Complete enhanced-ACT passage set: one original natural science passage of about 600 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000031) on urban heat islands (causes, unequal effects, reflective roofs, street trees), with 9 questions (Key Ideas and Details 3, Craft and Structure 4, Integration 2). Factual claims kept to well-established points (night-time peak, heat storage by paved surfaces, evaporative cooling by vegetation, climate-dependent effect of reflective roofs). Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: R031-01 hard→medium, R031-02 hard→medium, R031-03 medium→easy, R031-04 medium→easy, R031-05 medium→easy, R031-06 hard→easy, R031-08 hard→easy, R031-09 medium→easy.

passages.title: The Island in the City
passages.text:
On a still summer evening, a thermometer in the center of a large city may read several degrees higher than one in the farmland a few miles away. The difference is not a quirk of a single instrument. Measured across many cities and many years, the pattern is consistent enough to have a name, the urban heat island, and it is usually strongest not in the afternoon, when the sun is high, but after dark. In a large city on a calm, clear night, the gap between downtown and the surrounding countryside can be considerably larger than it is at midday, and it tends to shrink when clouds or a strong wind move in.

That timing is a clue to the cause. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them and store the energy as heat. A field of grass or a stand of trees absorbs sunlight too, but plants also release water vapor through their leaves, and turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air. A city has replaced much of that cooling vegetation with materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by trapping some of the heat that the streets radiate upward, and engines, air conditioners, and furnaces add heat of their own.

The consequences are not evenly shared. Within a single city, temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next, and the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement. Because heat that lingers into the night denies the body a chance to recover, these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave, especially for older residents and for people without air conditioning.

One response has been to make surfaces reflect more sunlight. A roof coated in a pale, reflective material can stay far cooler on a sunny afternoon than a dark one, and some cities now require or encourage such roofs on new buildings. The idea is simple, but its effects depend on circumstances. In a place with hot summers and mild winters, a reflective roof saves energy that would have gone to cooling. In a place with long, cold winters, the same roof also reflects sunlight that would have helped warm the building, and part of the summer savings may be lost.

Trees offer a different kind of help. A street tree shades the pavement beneath it, so less sunlight is stored in the first place, and it cools the air through its leaves. Unlike a coating, though, a tree takes years to grow, needs water and room for its roots, and can be lost to drought or disease. Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees. Many cities now try to do both.

Researchers continue to argue about how much each measure can accomplish, and the answer clearly varies from city to city. What is no longer in dispute is the basic picture: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it, which means that it can also be changed by the choices made in rebuilding it.

candidates.subskill: Central idea of an informational passage
candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Cities are hottest after dark because pavement releases the heat it stored by day.
choices.B: Reflective roofs and street trees both cool cities, though trees take longer to help.
choices.C: City temperatures depend partly on how cities are built, so rebuilding can lower them.
choices.D: Some neighborhoods are much hotter than others, which puts certain residents at risk.

candidates.evidence: a city's temperature is partly a product of the choices made in building it
candidates.explanation: Each wrong choice states a true point from one part of the passage. Only C covers the causes (how cities are built) and the responses (rebuilding), the point the last paragraph draws together.

A.rationale: This is the explanation in paragraphs 1 and 2, not the idea the whole passage builds to.

hints: Which choice covers the causes and the responses together?

strategy.explanation: Summarize each paragraph, then find the choice that covers all of them.

candidates.remember: When every choice is true, pick the one that covers the whole passage.

candidates.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the explanation for the urban heat island given in paragraph 2?

choices.A: At midnight, a dark-paved block is warmer than a nearby pale-paved block with the same trees.
choices.B: At noon, the center of a city is a few degrees warmer than the farmland a few miles away.
choices.C: At midnight, a large park in a city is about as warm as a nearby parking lot.
choices.D: In winter, a city's furnaces add far more heat to the outdoor air than its cars do.

candidates.evidence: materials that soak up heat all day and give it back slowly through the night
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says surfaces such as asphalt store the day's heat and release it at night. A night-time difference between dark and pale pavement, with trees held equal, isolates that cause.

B.rationale: This shows a daytime difference but says nothing about stored heat released at night.

C.rationale: This would weaken the explanation, which predicts the park would be cooler.

D.rationale: This concerns waste heat in winter, not the storage of sunlight by surfaces.

hints: What does paragraph 2 say causes the night-time warmth?

strategy.explanation: Ask which finding isolates the cause the author names.

candidates.remember: Strong evidence changes one factor while keeping the others the same.

candidates.stem: The author mentions that plants release water vapor through their leaves (paragraph 2) mainly to:

choices.A: show that plants absorb less sunlight than asphalt and brick do.
choices.B: suggest that cities should water their lawns and parks more often.
choices.C: introduce the health risks that heat brings to older residents.
choices.D: help explain why replacing vegetation with pavement makes a city warmer.

candidates.evidence: turning liquid water into vapor uses energy that would otherwise warm the air
candidates.explanation: The detail explains how vegetation cools the air, so replacing it with heat-storing materials removes that cooling and helps make the city warmer.

A.rationale: The passage says plants absorb sunlight too; the point is their cooling, not their absorption.

C.rationale: Health risks come in paragraph 3 and are not linked to water vapor.

hints: What does the city replace plants with?

strategy.explanation: Ask why the detail sits in a paragraph about causes.

candidates.remember: A detail usually supports the paragraph's main point.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word carry most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: these blocks can carry real risks to health during a heat wave
candidates.explanation: Blocks that 'carry real risks' present or pose those risks to their residents.

A.rationale: This is the common meaning, but nothing is being moved.

C.rationale: This would mean holding up a weight, which does not fit risks.

D.rationale: This sense, as in carrying an election, does not fit risks.

hints: Try each choice in the sentence.

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own, then match.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the sentence, not the most common one.

candidates.subskill: Applying the passage to a new case
candidates.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following places would most likely be the warmest at midnight during a summer heat wave?

choices.A: A block of apartments in the city center surrounded by parking lots and almost no trees
choices.B: A downtown block of tall office buildings with wide sidewalks lined by large shade trees
choices.C: A suburban street of houses with dark roofs set among tall, closely spaced shade trees
choices.D: A neighborhood at the edge of the city next to open farmland, with lawns and gardens

candidates.evidence: the hottest blocks are often those with the fewest trees and the most pavement
candidates.explanation: The passage links night-time heat to pavement that stores heat and to a lack of trees. The apartment block has both, with no trees to offset it; each other place has a heating feature offset by vegetation.

B.rationale: Tall buildings trap heat, but the shade trees reduce stored heat and cool the air.

C.rationale: Dark roofs store heat, but the dense trees shade them and cool the air.

D.rationale: Areas near farmland with vegetation are cooler than the city center.

hints: Which place has heat-storing surfaces with nothing to offset them?

strategy.explanation: Weigh heating features against cooling features for each place.

candidates.remember: Weigh every feature the author names, not just one.

candidates.subskill: Applying a qualified claim to choose a setting
candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 4, a reflective roof would most likely produce the greatest net energy savings over a year in which of the following places?

choices.A: A desert city where summers are long and very hot and frosts are rare
choices.B: A northern city with brief, warm summers and months of snow
choices.C: A city with very hot summers and long winters with heavy snow
choices.D: A coastal city that stays cool and overcast for most of the year

candidates.evidence: In a place with long, cold winters, the same roof also reflects sunlight that would have helped warm the building
candidates.explanation: A reflective roof saves cooling energy in hot weather but loses some of that saving in cold weather. The desert city has the most hot weather and almost no cold season.

B.rationale: Long winters there would cancel much of the small summer benefit.

C.rationale: The long cold season would cancel part of the large summer savings.

D.rationale: With little strong sun, a reflective roof has little to reflect in any season.

hints: What does a reflective roof gain in summer and lose in winter?

strategy.explanation: Weigh the summer gain against the winter loss for each place.

candidates.remember: Weigh both sides of a trade-off the author describes.

candidates.subskill: Linking a cause to a stated consequence
candidates.stem: The author's statement that heat lingering into the night "denies the body a chance to recover" (paragraph 3) helps explain why:

choices.A: older residents are less likely than other residents to own air conditioners.
choices.B: temperatures can differ sharply from one neighborhood to the next.
choices.C: reflective roofs work better in some climates than they do in others.
choices.D: the heat island's timing makes it especially harmful to health.

candidates.evidence: Because heat that lingers into the night denies the body a chance to recover
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the heat island is strongest after dark; paragraph 3 says heat that lingers into the night prevents the body from recovering. Together they explain why the effect is a health risk.

A.rationale: The passage names older residents as at risk but never says they lack air conditioning.

B.rationale: The statement concerns why heat harms people, not why neighborhoods differ.

C.rationale: Roof performance is the subject of paragraph 4, not this statement.

hints: When is the heat island strongest, according to paragraph 1?

strategy.explanation: Connect paragraph 3's statement to paragraph 1's timing.

candidates.remember: Link a consequence to a pattern described earlier.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 5, planners who think in decades most likely favor trees because they believe that:

choices.A: trees cost much less to plant than the coatings that are applied to roofs.
choices.B: over many years, a tree's slow start matters less than its two benefits.
choices.C: coatings cannot be applied to buildings that have already been built.
choices.D: trees, unlike roof coatings, can never be lost to drought or disease.

candidates.evidence: Planners who want quick results may favor coatings; planners who think in decades often favor trees.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 lists a tree's two benefits (shade and cooling) and its main drawback (it takes years to grow). Over decades the slow start matters less, so long-range planners favor trees.

D.rationale: Paragraph 5 says trees can be lost to drought or disease.

hints: What is the drawback of trees, and why would it matter less over decades?

strategy.explanation: Contrast quick results with a long time span.

candidates.remember: A drawback that is about time matters less over a long period.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?

choices.A: It presents a theory, tests it against new measurements, and finally rejects it.
choices.B: It describes a pattern, explains its causes and effects, and weighs two responses.
choices.C: It compares two particular cities and recommends the policies of one of them.
choices.D: It traces an idea's history from its first discovery up to the present day.

candidates.evidence: Trees offer a different kind of help.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the heat island, paragraph 2 its causes, paragraph 3 its effects, paragraphs 4 and 5 two responses (reflective roofs and trees), and paragraph 6 a conclusion.

A.rationale: The passage never rejects its explanation.

C.rationale: No particular cities are named or compared.

D.rationale: The passage gives no history of the idea's discovery.

hints: Write one word for each paragraph's job.
candidates.remember: An organization question asks about the order of jobs, not topics.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves (both matched every key) rated 8 of 9 items easy, with keys restating single sentences (01, 02, 05, 06, 09), a hedged-only key (07), throwaway distractors, and overlapping pairs (06/07, 01/09). Rebuilt 01 (all distractors true but partial), 02 (evidence evaluation), 05 (traps balancing heating and cooling features), 06 (climates described in new words), 07 (replaced by a cross-paragraph consequence item) and 09 (replaced by an organization item). Passage unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.
